Another card is almost always better than a similar option in nearly all scenarios. The fact that a mono-red deck can easily lose to a specific card that counters spells without green for the better option is significant, especially if it's commonly included in sideboards in your local area.

If you want your deck to be competitive, I would recommend acquiring a set of certain fetch lands now before their prices increase if you don't already own them. A few shock lands to fetch shouldn't be too costly to add, and you don't necessarily need a specific fetch land since you generally want lands that produce red mana on their own. Even if you stick with mono-red, you'd likely want fetch lands to enable certain spells, especially at instant speed. They are also quite beneficial if you plan to include a specific creature in your deck.

They don't have time during normal rounds to go in-depth and review every detail of a situation that was already handled by a lower-level official. If a ruling takes 10 minutes and then an appeal is made, they have to find the high-level official and come make a further ruling, which could take at least another 5-10 minutes without going over all the details again. That's one single match. Now consider there are hundreds of matches happening simultaneously in that round and there are several more rounds in the event that need to occur afterward. You can't realistically take that much time and delay future rounds by hours because of rulings and appeals; it's just not feasible for hosting the entirety of an event. The fact that there's even the option of appealing a ruling and getting a high-level official to come for any and all rulings throughout an entire tournament is already impressive. Look at other sports where you either can't appeal rulings made during a match or if you can, it's only during specific parts of the game. And in those cases, you're only talking about a single match happening at once, not hundreds.

Not to mention this whole scenario seems like it came down to miscommunication between a lower-level official and the head official. If you've never been to a large event, you have to realize things will be noisy. When you're talking about someone in charge of managing all the other officials and making final rulings, you aren't paying attention to all the noise around you to hear if others are commenting quietly that it was a token creature. Details can easily get missed in the chaos. Officials are people too and can make mistakes.

I think people are missing part of the point here. They aren't saying that the recent ban wasn't warranted. They're saying that if there wasn't a modern tournament series, they wouldn't be as concerned about there being a "best deck" that is consistently top tier and warps the meta-game around it. The point is it looks bad for the format for a specific deck to be such a consistently dominating presence that everyone has to constantly be aware of and play around specifically. If you weren't prepared for that match-up, your deck just wasn't competitive. This makes for bad coverage at the tournament level and makes modern less appealing for people to get into, which is bad PR for the game publisher. This doesn't mean that the deck isn't ban-worthy as well; it's just that if there was no modern tournament series, they would be much less concerned about making any bannings at all except for things that are huge problems or mistakes. I suspect if there was no modern tournament series, instead of these bannings, we'd be much more likely to simply see zero bans or unbans.

The hz of the display (60hz) is the refresh rate of the display. This indicates how often it refreshes the pixels/display. You don't change this when you're playing a game; it's determined by the hardware of your display. The framerate of a game is how many frames per second the game is producing. You want the framerate to be a multiple of the refresh rate because otherwise, it can lead to issues. If you're playing at 30fps on a 60hz display, that means that your screen is refreshing twice for each frame. Each frame is shown for 2 refreshes. If you have 45 frames per second but are refreshing 60 times per second, some frames are displayed for 2 refreshes and others for 1 refresh. This results in a poor visual experience.

The real issue with expandable memory options like micro-SD cards (and game cartridges being essentially a modified micro-SD card format) is that the format is VERY slow. Even the highest-end micro-SD cards (which cost significantly more than typical options for 128GB or 200GB) are barely on par with hard drive read/write speeds. This was never a problem when playing on previous handheld systems (unless you had a particularly low-quality micro-SD card), but if the company wants to push larger games and third-party titles, it's going to be a significant issue. Users will experience incredibly slow load times. Additionally, micro-SD cards are NOT designed for intensive read/write use, and using them for gaming frequently will lead to rapid deterioration, risking the loss of all save data.

Current gaming consoles are starting to include hybrid drives to address slow loading times, and it's easy to upgrade systems to use true solid-state drives for considerable improvements in load times. A solid-state drive typically has at least 5 times the speed of a hard drive, and some can reach speeds of over 3000 MB/s for reading and nearly 2000 MB/s for writing, compared to the highest-end micro-SD cards where maximum speeds are around 95 MB/s.

I am genuinely concerned about games where every loading screen lasts over 2 minutes.

If the actual console comes with a 32GB solid-state drive, that's even worse. The onboard memory would be at least 5 times faster than any expandable memory we could add. Forcing users to store games on their own added memory will lead to a much worse experience.

Players who opt for digital versions of games will face significant challenges. A typical third-party game easily exceeds 20-40GB (with some titles reaching up to 54GB). This means users may not even be able to install a single game on the console's built-in memory. If the cartridges are indeed a variant of micro-SD card technology, do we really expect third-party developers to sell games on a memory card that costs over $40? It’s likely we’ll end up with cartridges that are essentially links to download the digital copy, requiring additional memory space.

If we expect to receive third-party games that are equivalent to those on current-generation consoles, they will almost certainly require downloading the game rather than running off the cartridge.

The issue is even the best microSD cards are at best 5x slower than pretty much the worst solid-state drives. The best microSD cards are barely on par with 5400 rpm hard disk drives. Load times will be abysmal.

The BEST microSD cards have read speeds that are nearly equivalent to those of a standard 5400 RPM hard disk drive. The maximum speed achievable with a microSD card is around 95 MB/s, while a 5400 RPM HDD typically offers read speeds between 50-150 MB/s, depending on the drive's capacity, as larger drives tend to have longer read times. However, this refers to the highest quality microSD cards, which can cost approximately $40 for 32GB and $100 for 128GB. If someone opts for the cheapest, largest microSD card available—often chosen by those who are not well-informed about specifications—they will likely experience significantly slower speeds. For instance, a popular handheld gaming device originally came with either a class 4 or class 10 microSD card, which would provide speeds of 4MB/s or 10MB/s, respectively. Class 4 cards are still very common in retail stores, making it easy for uninformed buyers to select a card that is five times slower than the lowest speeds of a 5400 RPM HDD. If the internal memory of the device utilizes NAND technology similar to that of solid-state drives, it is likely at least five times faster than the best available microSD cards. The A1 standard, which claims to boost performance to "near-SSD levels," is still not particularly impressive, especially considering that top-tier SSDs are achieving speeds over six times greater than standard SSDs.

Additionally, microSD cards are not designed for frequent or constant read/write operations, and using them in such a manner will significantly reduce their lifespan, which is already not particularly long.

And by "decent" you mean top of the line ~$40 for 32GB (might not even be big enough for a single big game). A parent or child buying a micro SD card in a store without knowing anything about them is going to end up with something like a class 10 card that only reads at 10 MB/s max. Not to mention a significant number of people upgrade their gaming consoles with a hybrid or SSD since they make it possible to do so. Even then, games frequently will have 30s+ load times, with drives that have 500-550 MB/s read speeds.

What's your advantage?

"Hone"/"Fortify" buffs stack with "spur" buffs, and you can stack multiple spur buffs, but only one hone/fortify buff on the same stat.

Hone buffs include: Hone Attack, Speed, Cavalry, Fliers, Armor.  
Fortify buffs include: Fortify Defense, Resistance, Cavalry, Fliers, Armor, dragons.  
Spur buffs include: Spur Defense, Resistance, Attack, Speed, "goad" for cavalry/fliers/armor, and "ward" for cavalry/fliers/armor.

So you can stack Hone Cavalry for +6 attack/speed with a Fortify Cavalry that gives +6 defense/resistance and stack that with any number of goad/ward/spur buffs, but you can't stack it with Hone attack/speed/defense/resistance.

"Defiant" skills as well as healer balm specials count as hone/fortify effects.

Basically, anything that visibly affects the stats you can only use one of, and they don't stack; it will just take whatever the best stat boost is. In combat buffs, you can stack as many as you want together.

So a team of four cavalry heroes all running Goad Cavalry and all within two squares of each other will each get +12 attack/speed in combat from three Goad Cavalry from each other. A team of four Hone Cavalry will just give +6 attack/speed to each adjacent cavalry hero at the start of the turn.

You didn't ask, but I thought I'd also mention that "blade" tomes only gain a bonus from visible stat boosts from the hone/fortify buffs; they don't gain anything from in-combat buffs.
